Overview

Overview This document explains how GhostLeaks is built and how it works internally — the request lifecycle, the data model, the breach-checking pipeline, and the security mechanisms underneath every feature. It’s written for whoever will run, extend, or evaluate the codebase: your own engineers, a technical buyer doing due diligence, or you.
For what each feature does and why, see FEATURE_GUIDE.md . For how to deploy it, see DEPLOYMENT.md . This document is about how it’s built.
1. Technology Stack

Layer Choice Why Small, explicit, no hidden magic — Web framework Flask 3.x every route is a plain function you can read top to bottom. SQLAlchemy’s engine abstraction Flask-SQLAlchemy 2.x, over means the same model code runs ORM / database PostgreSQL (production) or SQLite against either database with one (local evaluation) connection-string change. Two different consumers (a human in a browser, a machine calling the Flask-Login (session cookies) + a API) get two different, purpose- Auth separate API-key path for the REST built auth mechanisms rather than API one mechanism stretched to cover both. Industry-standard adaptive Password hashing Flask-Bcrypt hashing; never reversible, never logged. No card data ever touches this Stripe Checkout (hosted page) + server — Stripe’s hosted page Payments webhooks handles that, and this app only ever sees a signed confirmation event. Email verification, password reset, Transactional email Brevo (Sendinblue) API and breach-alert emails.

Pluggable provider modules See §5 — no single vendor is Breach intelligence (BreachDirectory, HIBP, hardcoded into the application LeakCheck, XposedOrNot) logic. Server-side rendering of tenant- PDF generation ReportLab branded exposure reports.
Flask-Limiter, in-memory by Rate limiting See §7. default, Redis-backed if REDIS_URL is set Standard production entry point WSGI server Gunicorn ( gunicorn app:app ).

The application is a single Flask app ( app.py ) — there is no microservice split, no message queue, no background worker process. Every request is handled synchronously, start to finish, by a Gunicorn worker. This is a deliberate simplicity choice: at the scale a single self-hosted deployment (or even a multi-tenant MSP deployment with dozens of client workspaces) actually runs at, a job queue adds operational complexity without a corresponding benefit. See §9 for where this stops being true.
2. Request Lifecycle
A typical browser request — say, a logged-in user running an email breach check — flows like this:

1. Gunicorn accepts the HTTP request and hands it to a Flask worker process. 2. Flask-Login resolves the session cookie to a User row ( load_user() ), making current_user available for the rest of the request. If there’s no valid session, current_user is an anonymous user and any @login_required route redirects to /login . 3. Flask-Limiter checks the request against the route’s configured rate limit (e.g. "30 per minute" on /check-email ) before the view function runs at all. Over the limit → an immediate 429 with Retry- After headers, no application logic executes. 4. CSRF protection (Flask-WTF) validates the submitted token against the session for any state-changing POST request that isn’t explicitly exempted (the two API-key-authenticated JSON endpoints are exempted, since they don’t use session cookies in the first place — see §6). 5. The view function runs: reads request.form / request.get_json() , does its work, and returns a response. 6.

@app.after_request attaches baseline security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options , HSTS, etc.) to every response before it goes back to the browser — this runs regardless of which route handled the request, so no route can accidentally ship without them.

For an API request ( X-API-Key header instead of a session cookie), steps 2–4 are replaced by require_api_key() : it hashes the provided key, looks up the matching User by that hash, and attaches it to request.api_user — the rest of the request proceeds identically.
3. Data Model
Six tables, all scoped to a tenant except where noted:

Tenant — one row per workspace/client company. Holds branding ( brand_name , primary_color , logo_url ), plan, and demo-mode state. This is the isolation boundary everything else hangs off of. User — belongs to exactly one tenant, has a role ( owner / admin / member ), a bcrypt password hash, an API key (stored as a SHA-256 hash — see §6), payment status, and webhook URL. ScanHistory — one row per breach check performed (email, password, or bulk), what it found, and when. This is usage data — “what was scanned.” CredentialFinding — one row per (tenant, email, breach source) combination, deduplicated and upserted on every re-scan rather than duplicated. This is state data — “what’s currently true about this exposure,” carrying a status lifecycle ( active → rotated / historical / accepted_risk / resolved ) and a confidence score. DomainMonitor + DomainEmployeeEmail — a company domain a tenant wants monitored as a whole, gated behind DNS-based ownership verification (§4), with individual employee emails tracked underneath it.

AuditLog — administrative and state-changing actions (logins, status changes, domain verification, branding changes, API key rotation, account deletion). Distinct from ScanHistory : this answers “who changed what,” not “what was scanned.”

Every table except Tenant itself carries a tenant_id foreign key, and every query in the codebase filters on it. This is enforced by code convention, not by a database-level policy (no Postgres row-level security) — see §9 for the implication of that.
4. Multi-Tenancy and Isolation

A tenant is created one of two ways: - Register with no invite link → a brand-new Tenant is created, and the registering user becomes its owner . - Register with ?tenant_slug=... (an admin’s invite link) → joins that existing tenant as a member .

From that point forward, every database query touching tenant-scoped data filters on current_user.tenant_id (or request.api_user.tenant_id for API calls). There is no code path anywhere in the application — UI or API — that returns data belonging to a different tenant. This is the single rule the whole multi-tenant model rests on, and it’s why the product can safely serve multiple unrelated client companies from one deployment.
5. The Breach-Checking Pipeline
This is the core of the product, and it’s built to be provider-agnostic on purpose.

Provider architecture: each breach-data source (BreachDirectory, HIBP, LeakCheck, XposedOrNot as shipped) is a small module in providers/ , implementing one shared interface defined in providers/base_provider.py . Which provider(s) are active is controlled entirely by the BREACH_PROVIDER environment variable — a single name, or a comma-separated list to run several at once. Adding a new data source later means writing one new provider module and adding one line to the factory function in app.py ; nothing else in the application needs to change.

What actually happens on a check: 1. aggregate_breach_sources(email) calls every currently-active provider. 2. Each provider returns a list of source names it found the email in, or signals it couldn’t respond ( check_failed ). 3. Results are tallied by source name across all providers — if two providers both report “LinkedIn,” that’s one finding with confirmed_by = 2 , not two separate findings. 4. compute_confidence() scores the finding: 60 as a base for a single-source hit, +20 per additional confirming source (capped at +40), +5 if the exposure has been outstanding over a year. With only one provider configured, no finding can ever be cross-confirmed, so everything caps at 60–65 — that’s the pipeline being honest about single-source confidence, not a bug. 5. The result is upserted into CredentialFinding , keyed on (tenant_id, email, source_name) — re-scanning the same email against the same source updates the existing row ( last_seen , confidence) instead of creating a duplicate, so status history (§3) survives repeat scans.

A hard rule that runs through every one of these code paths: the actual leaked password or credential value is never read out of a provider’s response, never stored, and never returned to a user — only the fact of exposure (which source, roughly when, how confident). Provider modules are written to not even parse that field out of the response. This is what makes the product a breach-notification tool rather than a credential- lookup tool, and it’s treated as non-negotiable — see SECURITY.md .

Domain-wide monitoring (§ in FEATURE_GUIDE.md ) runs the same pipeline once per tracked employee email, rather than trying to check a bare domain string — breach providers index individual addresses, not domains, so that’s what actually finds real exposures. It’s gated behind a live DNS TXT-record check before any domain-wide scan is allowed to run, so a tenant can’t enumerate exposure data for a domain it doesn’t control.
6. Authentication and API Security
Session-based (browser) auth: standard Flask-Login session cookies, hardened with HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , and Secure (over HTTPS). CSRF tokens are required on every state-changing form
submission.

API-key auth: a key is generated the first time a user visits Settings ( gl_ prefix + 48 hex characters), and can be regenerated at any time, immediately invalidating the old one. Keys are stored as a SHA-256 hash — the raw value is shown exactly once, at generation time, and is never recoverable from the database afterward. The two REST endpoints that use this ( /api/v1/check-email , /api/v1/check-password ) are explicitly exempted from CSRF checks, since CSRF protection exists to defend session-cookie auth specifically — a request authenticated by a header the browser doesn’t attach automatically isn’t vulnerable to the cross-site form-submission attack CSRF tokens defend against.

Outbound webhooks: before every send (not just when the URL is first saved), the destination hostname is resolved and checked against private/loopback/link-local/reserved IP ranges, and the outbound request has redirects disabled. Both exist to close a specific gap: a hostname can resolve to a public IP when saved and a private one later (DNS rebinding), and requests follows redirects by default, which would otherwise let an allowed https:// host 30x to an internal address.

Payment webhook: Stripe webhook payloads are verified against their signature (using STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET ) before being trusted — an unsigned or incorrectly-signed request is rejected outright, so activation can’t be triggered by anyone who doesn’t hold Stripe’s actual signing secret.

Scheduled-job auth: the breach-alert cron endpoint ( /send-breach-alerts ) is protected by a shared secret compared using hmac.compare_digest (constant-time, to avoid timing attacks) and passed via a custom header rather than a query parameter — query parameters end up in server logs and browser history, a header does not.
7. Rate Limiting

Flask-Limiter enforces per-route limits (e.g. 10 registrations/hour, 30 checks/minute, 3 bulk scans/day) to prevent abuse and control third-party provider API spend. By default this state lives in-memory inside each Gunicorn worker process — which means the effective limit is roughly the configured value multiplied by however many workers are running, and resets whenever a worker restarts. Setting REDIS_URL switches to a shared Redis-backed store, giving accurate limits across every worker and every restart. For a single-worker deployment this distinction doesn’t matter; for anything scaled beyond one worker, Redis is the correct configuration, not an optional upgrade.
8. Payment Architecture

Stripe Checkout is used as a hosted page, not a custom card form — the browser is redirected to a page Stripe controls, and this application never sees, handles, or stores any card data. Two things happen on the way there and back:

/create-checkout-session creates a Stripe Checkout Session tied to current_user , recording which order belongs to which user before redirecting. /webhooks/stripe receives Stripe’s checkout.session.completed event, verifies its signature, and only then marks the user is_paid .

Activation is driven entirely by the webhook, not by a client-side “payment succeeded” callback — a webhook still fires even if the customer’s browser closes or their network drops right after paying, and a webhook can’t be forged into activating an account that didn’t actually pay, the way a client-side callback could be. Price and currency are read from environment variables ( PLAN_AMOUNT_CENTS , PLAN_CURRENCY , PLAN_PRICE_LABEL ) — nothing is hardcoded, so a deployment can price itself in any Stripe-supported currency without a code change.
9. Known Architectural Boundaries
Every system has edges. These are the ones worth knowing before you extend or scale this one:

No database migration tool. Schema changes rely on db.create_all() , which creates missing tables but never adds a missing column to a table that already has data in it. A fresh deployment is unaffected; an existing production database needs the exact ALTER TABLE statement run manually for each schema change (documented per-change in DEPLOYMENT.md ). Adopting a migration tool (e.g. Flask- Migrate/Alembic) is the natural next step if the schema will keep evolving. No database-level tenant isolation. Isolation is enforced by every query filtering on tenant_id in application code, not by a Postgres row-level security policy. For most deployments this is sufficient; if you’re serving mutually distrustful tenants at a scale where a single missed filter would be catastrophic, RLS is a reasonable second line of defense to add. No background job queue. Bulk CSV scans and the scheduled breach-alert job run synchronously, inside the request or cron-triggered request itself.

This is fine at the scale currently tested; a very large bulk upload or a very large user base on the scheduled job could approach a request timeout before a queue-based redesign becomes necessary. Rate-limit storage defaults to in-memory (see §7) — correct for a single worker, needs REDIS_URL beyond that. No automated test suite. Changes are verified by static syntax/import checks and manual testing, not a CI test suite exercising application behavior.

None of these are defects — they’re the tradeoffs of a codebase sized correctly for what it actually needs to do today, documented honestly so whoever operates or extends it knows exactly where the edges are.

Overview

GhostLeaks Enterprise Edition is a self-hosted SaaS platform that monitors emails, passwords, and company domains for exposure in known data breaches. It is sold as commercial source code: you deploy it under your own brand, connect your own breach-intelligence provider(s), and run it on your own infrastructure or your customers’.
It is built for:

MSPs and cybersecurity agencies offering breach monitoring as a managed service to clients, under their own name. Software agencies and SaaS companies that want to embed breach monitoring as a feature without building the provider integrations, scoring logic, or multi-tenancy from scratch. Internal security teams monitoring their own organization’s domain and staff accounts.
This document is the top-level overview. For deployment, see DEPLOYMENT.md ; for what you’re licensing, see LICENSE.md ; for a buyer-oriented walkthrough, see BUYER_GUIDE.md .

Deployment
Full instructions are in DEPLOYMENT.md . Summary:

Runs behind Gunicorn in production ( gunicorn -c gunicorn_config.py app:app ). Works with SQLite out of the box for evaluation; use a managed PostgreSQL database for production. Scheduled monitoring requires an external scheduler. The application does not run its own background job scheduler — GET /send-breach-alerts (protected by the X-Alert-Secret header) must be called periodically by something outside the app itself: your host’s cron/scheduled-job feature, a cron container, or an external uptime/cron service. Docker deployment is supported: Dockerfile , docker-compose.yml , and .env.example are included in the project root. docker compose up -d builds the app image, starts a bundled PostgreSQL container, waits for it to be healthy, then starts the app.
Domain Monitoring Workflow

1. Add a domain. An admin-level user (see Security for current role definitions) adds a company domain. A random verification token is generated. 2. Verify ownership. The workspace publishes a DNS TXT record at _ghostleaks-verify.<domain> with the value ghostleaks-verify=<token> . GhostLeaks performs a live DNS lookup; the domain is only marked verified on a match. 3. Add employee emails. Once verified, individual employee emails can be added to the domain. 4. Scan. Each tracked employee email is checked individually against the configured provider(s) and results are rolled up under the domain. If no employee emails have been added yet, the scan falls back to checking the bare domain name as a search term — breach providers index individual emails rather than domain names, so this fallback rarely returns meaningful results and exists only as a safety net, not as the primary mechanism.
Security Highlights

Passwords are checked using k-Anonymity; the full password is never transmitted. Breach provider responses are filtered before reaching any template or API response — only exposure metadata (source, confidence, status) is ever surfaced, never a credential value. Domain-wide scans require DNS-verified ownership before they can run. CSRF protection is applied to state-changing forms.
Full detail, including current gaps and known limitations, is in SECURITY.md .

Webhook Overview

Each user may configure one webhook URL (in Settings). When a new breach is detected for that user via the API or the scheduled alert job, GhostLeaks sends a JSON payload to that URL. See API.md for the payload shape.
Multi-Tenancy

Every customer-facing record (users, domains, findings, scan history) is scoped by tenant_id . Registering without an invite link creates a new, isolated tenant with that user as owner ; registering via a workspace’s invite link ( /register?tenant_slug=... ) joins that existing tenant as a member . There is no cross-tenant data access at the query layer.
White-Label Customization

Each tenant can set a brand name, primary color, and logo URL from the Workspace settings page. These values are applied across the dashboard, timeline, and PDF reports for that tenant only — other tenants on the same deployment are unaffected.

Pages that exist before anyone logs in — the landing page, login, register, pricing, and the other public pages — aren’t tied to any single tenant, so per-tenant branding doesn’t apply to them. These use DEFAULT_BRAND_NAME , DEFAULT_BRAND_COLOR , and DEFAULT_BRAND_LOGO instead (see Environment Variables). If a deployment is dedicated to a single company rather than run as multi-tenant SaaS, setting these three variables rebrands every pre-login page with no code changes required.
Demo Mode

From Workspace Settings, the workspace owner can load a full set of realistic demo data into their own tenant for demonstrations, screenshots, or evaluation — a sample company (“Acme Technologies,” green branding), five demo users, a pre-verified demo domain with those users tracked as employees, roughly a dozen credential findings across multiple sources and every status value, several weeks of scan history, and matching audit log activity.

Every row this creates is tagged internally as demo data and scoped to that tenant only. “Remove Demo Workspace” deletes exactly those rows and restores the tenant’s real branding — it never touches real data,

and never affects any other tenant. See SECURITY.md for the safety guarantees and DEPLOYMENT.md for the required one-time migration if you’re adding this to an existing deployment that already has data.

2. Feature Guide

Feature Guide This document walks through every feature in GhostLeaks Enterprise Edition: what it does, why it exists, and how to use it — for you as the operator, and for the end users on your deployment. Pair this with API.md if you’re integrating the REST API into your own product, and BUYER_GUIDE.md for how to position and sell this to your own customers.
Who This Is For — and What You Save

MSPs and cybersecurity agencies. You already sell security services — this gives you a breach-monitoring line item to add to every client contract without building one from scratch. A production-ready version of this (multi-tenant isolation, domain-ownership verification, confidence scoring, PDF reporting, white-labeling, an audit trail, and the security hardening documented in SECURITY.md ) is realistically months of engineering time if built in-house, not a weekend project. You’re buying that time back. Because it’s multi-tenant, one deployment serves every client you have — you’re not standing up infrastructure per client, so your hosting cost stays roughly flat as you add clients, while your billable line item scales per client.

Software agencies and SaaS companies. If you’re building breach-checking into an existing product, the REST API (§13) is a working integration surface on day one — email check, password check, risk score, all key-authenticated — instead of you writing your own provider integration, confidence-scoring logic, and rate- limiting from scratch. The multi-provider architecture (§19) means adding a second breach-data source later is one new file, not a rearchitecture.

Internal security teams. The realistic comparison here isn’t “build it yourself,” it’s the commercial breach- monitoring SaaS tools already on the market — most of which charge recurring per-seat or per-domain fees indefinitely. This is a one-time license instead of an ongoing subscription, and because it’s self-hosted, your employees’ email addresses and exposure data never leave your own infrastructure to sit in a third-party
vendor’s database — which itself simplifies any internal data-handling or vendor-risk review you’d otherwise have to go through to approve a SaaS tool.

Across all three: you’re also getting the parts that are easy to skip when building something like this quickly but expensive to bolt on later — tenant isolation enforced at the query level, domain-ownership verification before any domain-wide scan runs, API keys stored as hashes rather than plaintext, SSRF- guarded outbound webhooks, and self-service GDPR export/delete (§17–18) that removes a data-protection objection before a security-conscious buyer even has to ask about it.
1. Accounts, Workspaces, and Tenants

What it is: Every user belongs to exactly one tenant (a workspace — typically one client company, or your own organization if you’re the only user). All data — findings, scans, domains, audit logs — is scoped to a tenant and can never leak across tenants.

Why it exists: This is what makes the product usable by an MSP or agency serving multiple clients from one deployment, or an internal security team that just wants a single isolated workspace. Tenant isolation is enforced by filtering every database query on tenant_id — see ARCHITECTURE.md for the underlying rule.
How to use it:

The first person to register with no invite link becomes the owner of a brand-new workspace. To bring teammates in, share your registration link with ?tenant_slug=your-workspace-slug appended (find your slug in Admin → Workspace Settings), or build an invite flow around it in your own frontend if you’re white-labeling. Roles: owner (one per workspace, full control, cannot be demoted), admin (can manage domains, branding, and members), member (can run scans and see their own data).
2. Email Breach Check
What it is: Checks a single email address against your configured breach-intelligence provider(s) and records the result.

Why it exists: This is the core product loop — a user wants to know “has my email shown up in a known breach,” and this answers that question with a status ( leaked / safe / check_failed ) and, if leaked, which source(s).

How to use it: Dashboard → email check box → enter address → submit. Result is saved to Scan History and, if leaked, creates or updates a row in Findings. A check_failed result (the provider didn’t respond) is deliberately shown differently from safe — a failed check is never silently treated as “nothing found,” because that would be a false negative masquerading as good news.
3. Password Breach Check

What it is: Checks whether a password has appeared in known breach dumps, using the Have I Been Pwned k-anonymity range API — only a 5-character SHA-1 prefix of the password ever leaves your server; the actual password is never transmitted or stored anywhere.
Why it exists: Complements the email check — an email can be “safe” while its password (reused elsewhere) is already compromised. This is a separate, valuable signal.

How to use it: Dashboard → password check box → submit. Only the result ( leaked: true/false , and how many times it’s been seen) is stored — never the password itself, not even masked; the stored input_val is literally * characters equal to the password’s length, for length-pattern purposes only.
4. Bulk CSV Scan
What it is: Upload a CSV of email addresses (up to 100 per scan, up to 3 scans per day per user, 1 MB file size cap) and check all of them in one pass.
Why it exists: For onboarding a client’s existing employee list, or checking a batch of addresses without one-by-one manual entry.

How to use it: Dashboard → Bulk Scan → upload a .csv with one email per line (quotes are stripped automatically). Results show per-email status and a leaked/safe/failed summary. The daily-3-scans cap and 1 MB size cap exist to stop a single upload from exhausting provider quota or server memory — increase the limits in app.py ( MAX_CSV_BYTES , the today_bulk >= 3 check) if your provider quota and infrastructure can support it.
5. Domain Monitoring
What it is: Ongoing, DNS-verified monitoring of an entire company domain — not just one person’s email.

Why it exists: The realistic version of “monitor our whole company,” done honestly: breach-intelligence providers index individual email addresses, not domain strings, so scanning the bare domain name rarely finds anything real. This feature verifies domain ownership first, then lets you add each employee’s actual email so the scan checks real, indexed addresses.
How to use it (as an admin):

1. Add the domain — Dashboard → Domains → enter example.com . This creates an unverified DomainMonitor row with a random verification token. 2. Verify ownership — add a DNS TXT record at _ghostleaks-verify.example.com with the value ghostleaks-verify=<token> shown on the page, then click Verify. This step exists specifically so a tenant can’t enumerate breach data for a domain it doesn’t control. 3. Add employee emails — once verified, paste a list of emails (comma- or newline-separated, up to 200 per submission). Anything not ending in @example.com is silently skipped and reported back as skipped — this keeps a domain’s tracked list scoped to that domain, on purpose. 4. Scan — Domains → Scan. If employee emails are tracked, every one of them gets checked individually and results roll up under the domain. If none are tracked yet, a best-effort fallback scans the bare domain string (rarely useful — the UI says so explicitly).
6. Findings

What it is: The persistent record of every discovered exposure — one row per (tenant, email, breach source) combination, deduplicated automatically. Each finding has a status you can move through a lifecycle: active → rotated / historical / accepted_risk / resolved .

Why it exists: A breach check is a point-in-time answer; Findings is what turns repeated checks into an ongoing security workload your team can actually track and close out — “we know about this, we changed the password, it’s resolved” — rather than re-discovering the same exposure every scan.

How to use it: Findings page → filter by status. Click into a finding to change its status. Only the finding’s owner or a tenant admin/owner can change status. Confidence score (0–100) increases with the number of independent providers that confirm the same exposure, and slightly with how long it’s been publicly exposed — see compute_confidence() in app.py if you want to tune the weighting.
7. Exposure Timeline
What it is: A chronological feed of every “discovered” and “status changed” event across a tenant’s findings.

Why it exists: Gives a manager or auditor a single view of “what happened, in order” — useful for board- level security reporting, or a client-facing evidence trail of what was found and when it was remediated.
How to use it: Timeline page (nav) or GET /api/timeline if you’re building your own view on top of it.
8. Executive Risk Score

What it is: A single 0–100 score (and Low/Medium/High/Critical label) per user, computed from their scan history: the ratio of leaked-to-total scans, the number of distinct breach sources involved, and how recently the most recent leak occurred.

Why it exists: Non-technical stakeholders don’t want a list of breach names — they want “how worried should I be, on one number.” This exists to answer that in a client-facing dashboard or report without requiring the viewer to interpret raw findings.

How to use it: Shown on the Dashboard automatically. Also available as GET /api/risk-score (session- authenticated) or GET /api/v1/risk-score (API-key authenticated) if you want to surface it in your own UI. The exact weighting is intentionally simple (see calculate_risk_score() ) — treat it as a directional indicator, not a certified risk metric, and say so to your own customers if you present it as such.
9. PDF Exposure Reports
What it is: A downloadable, tenant-branded PDF summarizing either a single email check or a full bulk-scan result.
Why it exists: End users and MSP clients frequently want something they can save, forward, or attach to a compliance file — a PDF is the lowest-friction “proof of check” artifact.

How to use it: After any email or bulk check, a “Download Report” action posts the result data to /download- report , which renders it server-side with ReportLab, using the tenant’s brand color, name, and logo. Every piece of user-controlled text in the PDF is XML-escaped before being placed into the ReportLab markup — this is a deliberate SSRF/injection guard (ReportLab’s markup will actually fetch an target if you don’t escape it) and should not be removed if you modify this code.
10. White-Label Branding
What it is: Per-tenant brand name, primary color, and logo, injected into every template a logged-in user sees.

Why it exists: This is the feature that makes the product resellable as “your own product” rather than “GhostLeaks with your logo bolted on” — an MSP’s client never sees the word “GhostLeaks” anywhere in their session.

How to use it: Admin (owner only) → Workspace Settings → set brand name, hex color, and logo URL. Logged-out pages (landing, login, register) use the deployment-wide default branding instead ( DEFAULT_BRAND_NAME / DEFAULT_BRAND_COLOR / DEFAULT_BRAND_LOGO environment variables), since those pages aren’t tied to any one tenant yet.
11. Demo Mode
What it is: One click populates your own workspace with realistic, clearly-tagged sample data — users, a

domain, findings, scan history, and audit log entries spanning a fabricated four weeks — for demos, screenshots, and evaluation. One more click removes exactly that data and restores your real branding.

Why it exists: You need to demo this product to prospects without either showing an empty dashboard or using real client data. Every row this creates is tagged is_demo=True and scoped to your tenant — removal only ever touches those exact rows, in your tenant, never anything else.
How to use it: Admin (owner only) → Workspace Settings → Load Demo Data / Remove Demo Data. Refuses to load twice in a row (avoids duplicate data) and refuses to remove when nothing is loaded.

Note for an existing deployment upgrading into a version that already has real data: Demo Mode added several is_demo columns and two Tenant columns. A fresh deploy gets these automatically from db.create_all() ; an existing database needs them added manually first — see DEPLOYMENT.md .
12. Audit Log

What it is: An admin-visible, per-tenant record of who did what, when — logins, logouts, findings status changes, domain additions, branding changes, API key regeneration, demo data load/remove, account deletions, and more.

Why it exists: Distinct from Scan History (which records what was scanned): this records administrative and state-changing actions, which is what a client or compliance reviewer actually wants when they ask “who changed this.”
How to use it: Admin → Audit Logs (owner/admin only), shows the most recent 200 entries for the tenant.
13. REST API (X-API-Key)
What it is: A small, deliberately scoped API surface — email check, password check, and risk score — authenticated with an X-API-Key header instead of a session cookie.

Why it exists: For embedding breach-checking into your own product rather than presenting the GhostLeaks UI directly — the primary integration path for software agencies and SaaS companies, per BUYER_GUIDE.md .

How to use it: Full endpoint reference, request/response shapes, and rate limits are in API.md . A key is auto-generated the first time a user visits Settings, and can be regenerated at any time (invalidating the old one immediately). Keys are stored as a SHA-256 hash, never in plaintext — the raw value is shown exactly once, at generation time.
14. Webhooks (Outbound)
What it is: When a breach is detected for a user (via manual check, scheduled alert, or API call), GhostLeaks can POST a JSON payload to a URL that user configured in Settings.
Why it exists: Lets a downstream system (Slack, a ticketing system, your own alerting pipeline) react to a breach the moment it’s found, instead of polling.

How to use it: Settings → Webhook URL (must be https:// ). Every send re-validates the URL is not pointing at a private/internal/loopback address immediately before sending, not just at save time — this guards against DNS-rebinding, where a hostname resolves to a public IP when saved but a private one (e.g. a cloud metadata endpoint) later. Redirects are disabled on the outbound request for the same reason.
15. Scheduled Breach Alerts

What it is: A route ( /send-breach-alerts ) that, when triggered, checks every verified non-demo user’s email against your breach providers and emails them if something new turned up since their last check.

Why it exists: This is what makes “we monitor you continuously” true rather than “we monitor you only when you happen to open the app.” It’s a route, not a background job — GhostLeaks does not run its own scheduler.

How to use it: You must trigger it yourself on a schedule — a cron job, your host’s scheduled-task feature, or an external uptime/cron service hitting the URL. Authenticated with a shared secret in a custom header ( X-Alert-Secret , matched against the ALERT_SECRET environment variable using a constant-time comparison) — not a query parameter, since query parameters leak into logs and browser history. See DEPLOYMENT.md §6 for a concrete cron example.
16. Billing (Stripe)
What it is: A one-time-payment upgrade flow using Stripe Checkout — a hosted payment page, not a custom card form — that marks a user is_paid once payment is confirmed.

Why it exists: The default gate for monetizing your own deployment directly (as opposed to charging customers outside the product entirely, e.g. as part of a services contract). Kept deliberately simple: one plan, one price, no subscription/metering logic, so it’s easy to replace if your pricing model is more complex.
How to use it:

1. Create your own Stripe account and get a secret key from Developers → API keys. 2. Set STRIPE_SECRET_KEY in your environment. 3. Add a webhook endpoint in Stripe pointing at https://<your-domain>/webhooks/stripe , listening for checkout.session.completed , and set the resulting signing secret as STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET . 4. Set PLAN_AMOUNT_CENTS , PLAN_CURRENCY , and PLAN_PRICE_LABEL to your own price — there is no hardcoded price or currency in the code. 5. Activation happens via the webhook, not a client-side callback — this is intentional; a client that never calls back (network drop, closed tab) doesn’t leave a paid customer un-activated, and a forged client- side “success” call can’t activate an account that didn’t actually pay.

Order-ownership binding and payment-ID uniqueness (each Checkout session is tied to the user who created it, and a given Stripe payment can only ever activate one account) carry over from the original Razorpay implementation’s security fixes — see CHANGELOG.md [1.0.1] and [1.0.2].
17. Self-Service Data Export (GDPR)
What it is: A logged-in user can download everything their account owns — profile fields, scan history, credential findings, audit-log entries — as a single JSON file, on demand.

Why it exists: A “right to access/portability” request is one of the first questions many buyers (especially UK/EU-facing ones) get asked, and being able to say “there’s a button for that” removes an objection during a sale. It’s genuinely self-service — no admin has to manually pull and send the data.
How to use it: Settings → “Export my data.” Never includes the password hash, API key hash, or any other user’s data.
18. Self-Service Account Deletion (GDPR)
What it is: A logged-in user can permanently delete their own account, after confirming their current
password.
Why it exists: The “right to erasure” counterpart to data export — same sales-objection reasoning.

How to use it: Settings → “Delete my account” → confirm password. Two situations are blocked outright, with a clear on-screen explanation, rather than silently working around them: - A workspace owner cannot self-delete while other members still exist in the tenant (would orphan the workspace — there is no ownership-transfer feature as of this writing). - A user who has added a monitored domain cannot self- delete until that domain is removed (the database foreign key from domain to the user who added it does not allow a dangling reference).

What actually happens on deletion: scan history (exclusively the user’s own) is hard-deleted. Credential findings and audit-log entries — shared organizational security data the rest of the tenant may still need — are kept, but the personal link to the deleted user is removed rather than the rows themselves.
19. Multi-Provider Breach Intelligence

What it is: The breach-checking backend supports more than one data provider at once (BreachDirectory, HIBP, LeakCheck, XposedOrNot as shipped), configured via BREACH_PROVIDER (a single name or comma- separated list).

Why it exists: A single provider’s coverage is incomplete, and its confidence ceiling is capped low on purpose (see Findings above) to reflect that honestly. Running more than one provider and letting findings get cross-confirmed is what earns a higher confidence score — and is a stronger sales pitch than “we use one API.”

How to use it: Set BREACH_PROVIDER=breachdirectory,hibp (etc.) and the matching API key environment variables for each. Adding a new provider entirely means writing one new providers/*.py module implementing the shared interface (see providers/base_provider.py ) and adding one line to _build_active_providers() in app.py — nothing else in the file needs to change.

3. System Architecture

Overview This document explains how GhostLeaks is built and how it works internally — the request lifecycle, the data model, the breach-checking pipeline, and the security mechanisms underneath every feature. It’s written for whoever will run, extend, or evaluate the codebase: your own engineers, a technical buyer doing due diligence, or you.
For what each feature does and why, see FEATURE_GUIDE.md . For how to deploy it, see DEPLOYMENT.md . This document is about how it’s built.
1. Technology Stack

Layer Choice Why Small, explicit, no hidden magic — Web framework Flask 3.x every route is a plain function you can read top to bottom. Two different consumers (a human in a browser, a machine calling the Flask-Login (session cookies) + a API) get two different, purpose- Auth separate API-key path for the REST built auth mechanisms rather than API one mechanism stretched to cover both. Industry-standard adaptive Password hashing Flask-Bcrypt hashing; never reversible, never logged. No card data ever touches this Stripe Checkout (hosted page) + server — Stripe’s hosted page Payments webhooks handles that, and this app only ever sees a signed confirmation event. Pluggable provider modules See §5 — no single vendor is Breach intelligence (BreachDirectory, HIBP, hardcoded into the application LeakCheck, XposedOrNot) logic. The application is a single Flask app ( app.py ) — there is no microservice split, no message queue, no background worker process. Every request is handled synchronously, start to finish, by a Gunicorn worker. This is a deliberate simplicity choice: at the scale a single self-hosted deployment (or even a multi-tenant MSP deployment with dozens of client workspaces) actually runs at, a job queue adds operational complexity without a corresponding benefit. See §9 for where this stops being true.
2. Request Lifecycle
A typical browser request — say, a logged-in user running an email breach check — flows like this:

1. Gunicorn accepts the HTTP request and hands it to a Flask worker process. 2. Flask-Login resolves the session cookie to a User row ( load_user() ), making current_user available for the rest of the request. If there’s no valid session, current_user is an anonymous user and any @login_required route redirects to /login . 3. Flask-Limiter checks the request against the route’s configured rate limit (e.g. "30 per minute" on /check-email ) before the view function runs at all. Over the limit → an immediate 429 with Retry- After headers, no application logic executes. 4. CSRF protection (Flask-WTF) validates the submitted token against the session for any state-changing POST request that isn’t explicitly exempted (the two API-key-authenticated JSON endpoints are

exempted, since they don’t use session cookies in the first place — see §6). 5. The view function runs: reads request.form / request.get_json() , does its work, and returns a response. 6. @app.after_request attaches baseline security headers (CSP, X-Frame-Options , HSTS, etc.) to every response before it goes back to the browser — this runs regardless of which route handled the request, so no route can accidentally ship without them.

For an API request ( X-API-Key header instead of a session cookie), steps 2–4 are replaced by require_api_key() : it hashes the provided key, looks up the matching User by that hash, and attaches it to request.api_user — the rest of the request proceeds identically.
3. Data Model
Six tables, all scoped to a tenant except where noted:

Tenant — one row per workspace/client company. Holds branding ( brand_name , primary_color , logo_url ), plan, and demo-mode state. This is the isolation boundary everything else hangs off of. User — belongs to exactly one tenant, has a role ( owner / admin / member ), a bcrypt password hash, an API key (stored as a SHA-256 hash — see §6), payment status, and webhook URL. ScanHistory — one row per breach check performed (email, password, or bulk), what it found, and when. This is usage data — “what was scanned.” CredentialFinding — one row per (tenant, email, breach source) combination, deduplicated and upserted on every re-scan rather than duplicated. This is state data — “what’s currently true about this exposure,” carrying a status lifecycle ( active → rotated / historical / accepted_risk / resolved ) and a confidence score. DomainMonitor + DomainEmployeeEmail — a company domain a tenant wants monitored as a whole, gated behind DNS-based ownership verification (§4), with individual employee emails tracked underneath it.

AuditLog — administrative and state-changing actions (logins, status changes, domain verification, branding changes, API key rotation, account deletion). Distinct from ScanHistory : this answers “who changed what,” not “what was scanned.”

Every table except Tenant itself carries a tenant_id foreign key, and every query in the codebase filters on it. This is enforced by code convention, not by a database-level policy (no Postgres row-level security) — see §9 for the implication of that.
4. Multi-Tenancy and Isolation

A tenant is created one of two ways: - Register with no invite link → a brand-new Tenant is created, and the registering user becomes its owner . - Register with ?tenant_slug=... (an admin’s invite link) → joins that existing tenant as a member .

From that point forward, every database query touching tenant-scoped data filters on current_user.tenant_id (or request.api_user.tenant_id for API calls). There is no code path anywhere in the application — UI or API — that returns data belonging to a different tenant. This is the single rule the whole multi-tenant model rests on, and it’s why the product can safely serve multiple unrelated client companies from one deployment.
5. The Breach-Checking Pipeline
This is the core of the product, and it’s built to be provider-agnostic on purpose.

Provider architecture: each breach-data source (BreachDirectory, HIBP, LeakCheck, XposedOrNot as shipped) is a small module in providers/ , implementing one shared interface defined in providers/base_provider.py . Which provider(s) are active is controlled entirely by the BREACH_PROVIDER

environment variable — a single name, or a comma-separated list to run several at once. Adding a new data source later means writing one new provider module and adding one line to the factory function in app.py ; nothing else in the application needs to change.

What actually happens on a check: 1. aggregate_breach_sources(email) calls every currently-active provider. 2. Each provider returns a list of source names it found the email in, or signals it couldn’t respond ( check_failed ). 3. Results are tallied by source name across all providers — if two providers both report “LinkedIn,” that’s one finding with confirmed_by = 2 , not two separate findings. 4. compute_confidence() scores the finding: 60 as a base for a single-source hit, +20 per additional confirming source (capped at +40), +5 if the exposure has been outstanding over a year. With only one provider configured, no finding can ever be cross-confirmed, so everything caps at 60–65 — that’s the pipeline being honest about single-source confidence, not a bug. 5. The result is upserted into CredentialFinding , keyed on (tenant_id, email, source_name) — re-scanning the same email against the same source updates the existing row ( last_seen , confidence) instead of creating a duplicate, so status history (§3) survives repeat scans.

A hard rule that runs through every one of these code paths: the actual leaked password or credential value is never read out of a provider’s response, never stored, and never returned to a user — only the fact of exposure (which source, roughly when, how confident). Provider modules are written to not even parse that field out of the response. This is what makes the product a breach-notification tool rather than a credential- lookup tool, and it’s treated as non-negotiable — see SECURITY.md .

Domain-wide monitoring (§ in FEATURE_GUIDE.md ) runs the same pipeline once per tracked employee email, rather than trying to check a bare domain string — breach providers index individual addresses, not domains, so that’s what actually finds real exposures. It’s gated behind a live DNS TXT-record check before any domain-wide scan is allowed to run, so a tenant can’t enumerate exposure data for a domain it doesn’t control.
6. Authentication and API Security
Session-based (browser) auth: standard Flask-Login session cookies, hardened with HttpOnly , SameSite=Lax , and Secure (over HTTPS). CSRF tokens are required on every state-changing form submission.

API-key auth: a key is generated the first time a user visits Settings ( gl_ prefix + 48 hex characters), and can be regenerated at any time, immediately invalidating the old one. Keys are stored as a SHA-256 hash — the raw value is shown exactly once, at generation time, and is never recoverable from the database afterward. The two REST endpoints that use this ( /api/v1/check-email , /api/v1/check-password ) are explicitly exempted from CSRF checks, since CSRF protection exists to defend session-cookie auth specifically — a request authenticated by a header the browser doesn’t attach automatically isn’t vulnerable to the cross-site form-submission attack CSRF tokens defend against.

Outbound webhooks: before every send (not just when the URL is first saved), the destination hostname is resolved and checked against private/loopback/link-local/reserved IP ranges, and the outbound request has redirects disabled. Both exist to close a specific gap: a hostname can resolve to a public IP when saved and a private one later (DNS rebinding), and requests follows redirects by default, which would otherwise let an allowed https:// host 30x to an internal address.

Payment webhook: Stripe webhook payloads are verified against their signature (using STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET ) before being trusted — an unsigned or incorrectly-signed request is rejected outright, so activation can’t be triggered by anyone who doesn’t hold Stripe’s actual signing secret.

Scheduled-job auth: the breach-alert cron endpoint ( /send-breach-alerts ) is protected by a shared secret compared using hmac.compare_digest (constant-time, to avoid timing attacks) and passed via a custom header rather than a query parameter — query parameters end up in server logs and browser history, a header does not.
7. Rate Limiting

Flask-Limiter enforces per-route limits (e.g. 10 registrations/hour, 30 checks/minute, 3 bulk scans/day) to prevent abuse and control third-party provider API spend. By default this state lives in-memory inside each Gunicorn worker process — which means the effective limit is roughly the configured value multiplied by however many workers are running, and resets whenever a worker restarts. Setting REDIS_URL switches to a shared Redis-backed store, giving accurate limits across every worker and every restart. For a single-worker deployment this distinction doesn’t matter; for anything scaled beyond one worker, Redis is the correct configuration, not an optional upgrade.
8. Payment Architecture

Stripe Checkout is used as a hosted page, not a custom card form — the browser is redirected to a page Stripe controls, and this application never sees, handles, or stores any card data. Two things happen on the way there and back:

/create-checkout-session creates a Stripe Checkout Session tied to current_user , recording which order belongs to which user before redirecting. /webhooks/stripe receives Stripe’s checkout.session.completed event, verifies its signature, and only then marks the user is_paid .

Activation is driven entirely by the webhook, not by a client-side “payment succeeded” callback — a webhook still fires even if the customer’s browser closes or their network drops right after paying, and a webhook can’t be forged into activating an account that didn’t actually pay, the way a client-side callback could be. Price and currency are read from environment variables ( PLAN_AMOUNT_CENTS , PLAN_CURRENCY , PLAN_PRICE_LABEL ) — nothing is hardcoded, so a deployment can price itself in any Stripe-supported currency without a code change.
9. Known Architectural Boundaries
Every system has edges. These are the ones worth knowing before you extend or scale this one:

No database migration tool. Schema changes rely on db.create_all() , which creates missing tables but never adds a missing column to a table that already has data in it. A fresh deployment is unaffected; an existing production database needs the exact ALTER TABLE statement run manually for each schema change (documented per-change in DEPLOYMENT.md ). Adopting a migration tool (e.g. Flask- Migrate/Alembic) is the natural next step if the schema will keep evolving. No database-level tenant isolation. Isolation is enforced by every query filtering on tenant_id in application code, not by a Postgres row-level security policy. For most deployments this is sufficient; if you’re serving mutually distrustful tenants at a scale where a single missed filter would be catastrophic, RLS is a reasonable second line of defense to add. No background job queue. Bulk CSV scans and the scheduled breach-alert job run synchronously, inside the request or cron-triggered request itself.

This is fine at the scale currently tested; a very large bulk upload or a very large user base on the scheduled job could approach a request timeout before a queue-based redesign becomes necessary. Rate-limit storage defaults to in-memory (see §7) — correct for a single worker, needs REDIS_URL beyond that. No automated test suite. Changes are verified by static syntax/import checks and manual testing, not a CI test suite exercising application behavior.

None of these are defects — they’re the tradeoffs of a codebase sized correctly for what it actually needs to do today, documented honestly so whoever operates or extends it knows exactly where the edges are. -e
4. REST API Reference

API Reference This document covers GhostLeaks Enterprise Edition’s REST API (for external integrations), its webhook payload format, and the internal session-based endpoints used by the web dashboard itself.
Authentication
The public REST API is authenticated with a per-user API key.

Every user has one API key, generated automatically on registration and viewable/regenerable from Settings. Send it as the X-API-Key request header on every call. Regenerating a key immediately invalidates the previous one — any integration using the old key will start receiving 401 Invalid API key until updated. API access requires the account to be on a paid plan; unpaid accounts receive 402 UPGRADE_REQUIRED .

Security Policy This document describes GhostLeaks Enterprise Edition’s security model, the protections already built into the codebase, known limitations, and how to report a vulnerability.

This document describes the security posture of the source code as licensed. It is not a certification, audit report, or compliance attestation. Licensee is responsible for its own security review, penetration testing, and compliance obligations before operating the Software in production — see LICENSE.md Section 6.

Built-in Security Measures
The following protections exist in the codebase as delivered. This list reflects what is actually implemented, not aspirational goals.
Credential handling

Passwords are checked via k-Anonymity. Only a 5-character SHA-1 prefix of the password is ever sent to the password-check provider (Have I Been Pwned’s range API); the full password never leaves the point where it is hashed.

Breach provider responses are filtered before use. Every provider implementation returns only a source name — never a password, hash, or other credential value from the underlying breach data. This is enforced at the provider layer ( providers/ ), not only in the UI, so it cannot be bypassed by a template change. Passwords are hashed with bcrypt ( Flask-Bcrypt ) before storage; plaintext passwords are never persisted.
Domain monitoring
Domain-wide monitoring requires DNS TXT ownership verification before any scan can run against a domain. A tenant cannot monitor a domain it hasn’t proven control of.
Webhooks (SSRF protections)
Webhook URLs are validated to reduce server-side request forgery risk:

Only https:// URLs are accepted. The resolved IP address(es) of the hostname are checked and rejected if private, loopback, link-local, reserved, or multicast (blocking access to internal networks and cloud metadata endpoints). This check is re-run immediately before every webhook send, not only when the URL is saved — this specifically defends against DNS rebinding, where a hostname resolves to a public address at save time and an internal address later. Redirects are disabled on the outbound webhook request ( allow_redirects=False ), so a webhook cannot be saved pointing at an allowed host and then redirect to an internal one at send time.
Session and request security

Session cookies are set HttpOnly and SameSite=Lax . SESSION_COOKIE_SECURE is enabled automatically unless FLASK_ENV=development is set. CSRF protection ( Flask-WTF ) is enabled on session-authenticated forms. The three /api/v1/* REST endpoints are explicitly exempted from CSRF, since they authenticate via the X-API-Key header rather than a session cookie. Request body size is capped ( MAX_CONTENT_LENGTH , 2 MB) to limit abuse via oversized uploads. Rate limiting ( Flask-Limiter ) is applied per-route (see API.md for the current per-endpoint limits) with a default fallback limit of 500/day and 100/hour per client IP. Security headers (v1.0.0) are set on every response via an after_request hook: X-Content-Type- Options: nosniff , X-Frame-Options: DENY , Referrer-Policy: strict-origin-when-cross-origin , Permissions-Policy , and a Content-Security-Policy . Strict-Transport-Security is added only when the request is already HTTPS, so it’s never sent on a plain-HTTP local/dev connection.

The CSP allows 'unsafe-inline' for scripts and styles because the UI’s existing inline <script> blocks and onclick handlers depend on it — tightening this to a nonce-based CSP would require reworking every template’s JavaScript, which was deliberately out of scope for the v1.0.0 launch (see ROADMAP.md ) to avoid regression risk. The scheduled-alert endpoint’s shared-secret check (v1.0.0) uses hmac.compare_digest() instead of != , avoiding a timing side-channel on the comparison. /health (v1.0.0) is an unauthenticated liveness/readiness endpoint for load balancers and uptime monitors — it checks the app is responding and the database is reachable, returning 503 if the database check fails. It intentionally reveals no information beyond up/down status. Payment ownership verification (v1.0.0): /verify-payment previously verified the Razorpay signature (proving {order_id, payment_id, signature} are mutually consistent) but never confirmed the order belonged to the account trying to redeem it. A valid triple obtained any way — including a leaked or shared one — could activate a different account.

Orders are now bound to the user who created them ( User.pending_order_id , set in /create-order ), checked before activation, and razorpay_payment_id is a unique database column so the same payment can never activate more than one account. Rate-limiter storage is now configurable (v1.0.0): set REDIS_URL to use a shared Redis backend instead of the default in-memory store, so limits are accurate across multiple Gunicorn workers or app instances rather than effectively multiplied by worker count. Unset by default — existing deployments are unaffected until this is explicitly configured.

API keys are hashed, not stored in plaintext (v1.0.0): new and regenerated API keys are stored as a SHA-256 hash; the raw value is shown once at generation time and cannot be retrieved from the database afterward. Keys issued before this change continue to work via a backward-compatible plaintext lookup path — no existing integration was broken by this change, but regenerating (recommended) upgrades that account to the newer storage.
Data isolation

Every tenant-scoped table (users, domains, findings, scan history) is queried with an explicit tenant_id filter. There is no code path that returns another tenant’s data by default. Database access is entirely through SQLAlchemy’s ORM query interface — there is no raw, string- concatenated SQL in the application.
Demo Mode

Restricted to the owner role, and every query it runs (both loading and removing demo data) is scoped to current_user.tenant — it cannot affect any other tenant on the deployment. Every row it creates is tagged is_demo = True . Removal deletes only rows with that tag for that tenant; no other data, demo or real, is ever touched. Demo user accounts ( *@acme-demo.com ) are created with a random, never-disclosed password hash — they cannot be logged into. They exist only to populate lists (Members, Findings, Audit Log), not as usable accounts. The tenant’s real branding (name, color, logo) is backed up before being overwritten with demo branding, and restored exactly on removal — never reset to a hardcoded default. Loading demo data twice is blocked by a demo_active flag on the tenant, rather than relying on the button being disabled client-side (which a direct POST request could bypass).
Audit trail

Account and workspace-level actions (registration, status changes, domain actions, branding changes, API key regeneration) are recorded in an admin-visible audit log, separate from per-user scan history.
Known Limitations
These are honest, current gaps — not omissions. Review them before relying on this Software for a security- sensitive deployment.

1. Role-based access control. owner , admin , and member roles are all reachable today. The workspace owner can promote a member to admin or demote an admin back to member from Workspace Settings ( /admin/tenant-settings ), which requires the owner role. An owner cannot change their own role through this control, and a member cannot self-promote — only the owner can change another member’s role, and every change is recorded in the audit log. 2. Rate limiting is in-memory, per-process. Flask-Limiter is configured with storage_uri="memory://" . Gunicorn typically runs multiple worker processes ( 2 * CPU + 1 by default, per gunicorn_config.py ), and each worker maintains its own independent rate-limit counters. This means the effective rate limit for a given client is roughly (configured limit) × (number of workers) , not the configured value exactly, and limits reset if a worker restarts. For accurate, shared rate limiting across workers or multiple app instances, point Flask-Limiter at a shared backend (e.g. Redis) instead. 3. Domain-wide scanning without employee emails is a weak fallback.

Once a domain is DNS- verified, scanning it without first adding employee emails falls back to searching the bare domain string against the configured provider(s) — which rarely returns meaningful results, since breach providers index individual emails rather than domain names. This is documented in-product; don’t present a domain scan as comprehensive coverage unless employee emails have been added. 4. Confidence scoring is only as strong as the number of active providers. With a single provider configured, no finding can be cross-confirmed, so confidence scores are honestly capped lower than they would be with multiple providers active. 5. No built-in background job scheduler. The scheduled breach-alert endpoint ( GET /send-breach-

alerts ) must be triggered by an external scheduler (host cron, a scheduled job service, etc.) — see DEPLOYMENT.md . 6. No dedicated Web Application Firewall, intrusion detection, or anomaly-detection layer is included. These are deployment-level concerns Licensee should address (e.g. a WAF or reverse proxy in front of the application) if required for its environment.
Dependency and Third-Party Risk

GhostLeaks depends on third-party services (breach-intelligence providers, payment processing, transactional email) and open-source Python packages (see requirements.txt ). Licensee is responsible for:

Keeping dependencies patched and up to date. Monitoring for vulnerabilities disclosed in dependencies (e.g. via pip-audit , Dependabot, or similar tooling — not currently configured in this project). Reviewing the terms, data handling practices, and security posture of any third-party provider it connects (see LICENSE.md Section 4).

6. Deployment Guide
Deployment Guide Two supported paths: Docker Compose (bundled PostgreSQL, recommended for most buyers) or a manual host deployment (your own Python environment and database). Both are covered below.
0. First hour — plain-language checklist
Do these in order, regardless of which deployment path you choose:

1. Get your accounts ready (10–15 min): a RapidAPI account with a BreachDirectory subscription (or an account with any other supported provider — see README.md ), a Brevo account for sending email, and — if not using the bundled Docker database — a PostgreSQL database (a managed provider such as Render or Supabase both work). 2. Fill in your environment variables. Copy .env.example to .env and fill in real values. At minimum: SECRET_KEY , ALERT_SECRET , at least one breach-provider key ( RAPIDAPI_KEY by default), BREVO_API_KEY , MAIL_USERNAME (an email address you actually control — the app will refuse to send email rather than silently use a placeholder address), and APP_PUBLIC_URL once you have a real domain. 3. Start the app and load it once — this triggers db.create_all() , which creates every required table automatically. 4. Register your own account through /register — you become the owner of a new workspace automatically. Check your email and click the verification link. 5. Set your branding at /admin/tenant-settings — your company name, primary color, and logo.

This is what your customers or employees see instead of default GhostLeaks branding. 6. If monitoring a company domain: add it under the Domains tab, publish the DNS TXT record it shows you, click “Check TXT” once it’s propagated (a few minutes to a couple of hours depending on your DNS provider), then add the domain’s employee emails so scans check something real — see README.md . 7. Wire up scheduled monitoring — point an external scheduler at GET /send-breach-alerts with header X-Alert-Secret: <your ALERT_SECRET> , once every 24 hours. See §6. 8. Invite your team — share the invite link on the Workspace Settings page; anyone who registers through it joins your workspace instead of creating a new one.
If something isn’t working, check the application logs first — most first-day issues are a missing or incorrect environment variable, and the app logs those explicitly rather than failing silently.
1. Option A — Docker Compose (recommended)
The project includes a Dockerfile , docker-compose.yml , and .env.example that together run the app alongside a bundled PostgreSQL container.
cp .env.example .env # edit .env — fill in SECRET_KEY, ALERT_SECRET, POSTGRES_PASSWORD, provider keys, etc. docker compose up -d
What this does:

Builds the app image from the included Dockerfile . Starts a postgres:16-alpine container using POSTGRES_USER / POSTGRES_PASSWORD / POSTGRES_DB from .env . Waits for the database to report healthy ( pg_isready ) before starting the app — docker-entrypoint.sh also waits for Postgres to accept connections before running Gunicorn. Builds DATABASE_URL automatically from the POSTGRES_* values, so you do not need to construct a connection string by hand. If you’d rather point at an external database instead of the bundled container, uncomment and set DATABASE_URL directly in .env — that value takes precedence. Exposes the app on ${APP_PORT:-5000} (default 5000 ) on the host.
To stop: docker compose down (add -v to also remove the database volume — this deletes your data, so only do this intentionally).

Gunicorn worker/thread/timeout tuning is read from GUNICORN_WORKERS , GUNICORN_THREADS , GUNICORN_TIMEOUT , and GUNICORN_LOG_LEVEL in .env — see gunicorn_config.py for the defaults used when these are left unset.
The container runs as a non-root user ( appuser ) as of v1.0.1 — no action needed on your part, this is just how the image is built now.

Optional: shared rate limiting with Redis. By default, rate limits are tracked in memory per Gunicorn worker, which means the effective limit is roughly the configured value multiplied by your worker count (see SECURITY.md ). If you’re running multiple workers or multiple app instances and want accurate shared limits, bring up the bundled Redis service and point the app at it:
docker compose --profile with-redis up -d

then set REDIS_URL=redis://redis:6379/0 in .env and restart the web service. A plain docker compose up -d (without --profile with-redis ) never starts Redis and behaves exactly as before — this is entirely opt-in.
2. Option B — Manual host deployment
pip install -r requirements.txt cp .env.example .env # fill in real values, including a real DATABASE_URL python3 app.py # local dev # or, in production: gunicorn -c gunicorn_config.py app:app

db.create_all() runs automatically on startup and creates any tables that don’t already exist. This is additive-only — it will not alter existing tables. If you are upgrading an existing production deployment rather than starting fresh, see §4 before deploying.
If you’re using SQLite (leave DATABASE_URL unset entirely) for evaluation, be aware that SQLite is a single file

on local disk — it will not survive a container restart on most hosting platforms unless you mount a persistent volume for it, and it is not a recommended production configuration. Use PostgreSQL for anything beyond local evaluation.

Pin your Python version. This app is built and tested against Python 3.11 (the Dockerfile uses python:3.11- slim ). If you’re deploying to a platform with a native Python buildpack instead of Docker (Render, Railway, Heroku-style hosts), that platform will default to whatever its latest Python is unless you tell it otherwise — which can be a version this app has never been tested against, and dependency wheels (especially psycopg / setuptools ) may not have compatible builds for it yet, causing install or startup failures that have nothing to do with your configuration. Add a runtime.txt file to the project root containing:
python-3.11.9

This is the single most common cause of “it worked locally but fails on my host” for buyers deploying without Docker — set this before anything else if you hit an install or startup error on a native-buildpack host.

If your database sits behind a connection pooler (e.g. Supabase’s pooled connection string, PgBouncer in transaction mode): the app connects using psycopg (v3), which uses server-side prepared statements by default. Transaction-mode poolers can reuse the same underlying connection across unrelated sessions, which can produce a DuplicatePreparedStatement error under load. If you see that error, either use your provider’s session-mode / direct connection string instead of the pooled one, or disable server-side prepares by adding this right after app.config['SQLALCHEMY_DATABASE_URI'] = database_url in app.py :
if database_url.startswith('postgresql+psycopg://'): app.config['SQLALCHEMY_ENGINE_OPTIONS'] = { 'connect_args': {'prepare_threshold': None} }

4. Upgrading an existing deployment

If you are upgrading from a version of this codebase that predates multi-tenancy (no Tenant , DomainMonitor , CredentialFinding , or AuditLog tables, and no tenant_id column on User / ScanHistory ), db.create_all() will create the new tables but will not add a tenant_id column to your existing user / scan_history tables or backfill it. Running it as-is against such a database will fail or leave rows inconsistent.
Recommended path:

1. Take a full database backup first. 2. Manually create one Tenant row representing your existing single-company deployment. 3. Add a nullable tenant_id column to user and scan_history , backfill every existing row with that tenant’s ID, then tighten the column to NOT NULL once backfilled. 4. Deploy normally — db.create_all() will create the remaining new tables.

This isn’t scripted here because it depends on your existing data shape. Treat it as a one-time manual migration; adopting Alembic before this point is a reasonable investment if you don’t already have a migration tool in place — see ARCHITECTURE.md for the current state of schema management ( db.create_all() only, no migration framework).
Required migration: Demo Mode columns

Demo Mode (see §9) added new columns to six existing tables. db.create_all() only creates missing tables, not missing columns on tables that already exist — if you’re upgrading a deployment that already has data, run this once against your database before Demo Mode will work (a fresh, brand-new deployment doesn’t need this — db.create_all() already includes these columns for tables it creates from scratch):

ALTER TABLE tenant ADD COLUMN demo_active BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE; ALTER TABLE tenant ADD COLUMN demo_branding_backup TEXT; ALTER TABLE "user" ADD COLUMN is_demo BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE; ALTER TABLE scan_history ADD COLUMN is_demo BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE; ALTER TABLE domain_monitor ADD COLUMN is_demo BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE; ALTER TABLE domain_employee_email ADD COLUMN is_demo BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE; ALTER TABLE credential_finding ADD COLUMN is_demo BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE; ALTER TABLE audit_log ADD COLUMN is_demo BOOLEAN DEFAULT FALSE;
Back up your database before running this, as with any schema change. "user" is quoted because user is a reserved word in PostgreSQL.
Required migration: API key hashing column

A separate fix stores API keys as a SHA-256 hash ( api_key_hash ) rather than relying solely on the plaintext api_key column. A fresh deployment already gets this column from db.create_all() ; an existing deployment with data needs it added manually before /settings or X-API-Key auth will work correctly:
ALTER TABLE "user" ADD COLUMN api_key_hash VARCHAR(64) UNIQUE;
Required migration: Stripe payment column

The payment provider was switched from Razorpay to Stripe. A fresh deployment gets the stripe_payment_id column automatically from db.create_all() ; an existing deployment (upgrading from a Razorpay-based version) needs it added manually, and the old Razorpay column dropped:
ALTER TABLE "user" ADD COLUMN stripe_payment_id VARCHAR(200) UNIQUE; ALTER TABLE "user" DROP COLUMN IF EXISTS razorpay_payment_id;
Required migration: Stripe payment column
Payments moved from Razorpay to Stripe. A fresh deployment already gets the right column from db.create_all() . An existing deployment that had the old razorpay_payment_id / pending_order_id
columns needs this run manually — old paid-user data is preserved, it’s just renamed:

ALTER TABLE "user" ADD COLUMN stripe_payment_id VARCHAR(200) UNIQUE; ALTER TABLE "user" DROP COLUMN pending_order_id; -- Optional cleanup once you've confirmed nothing else reads the old column: -- ALTER TABLE "user" DROP COLUMN razorpay_payment_id;

You’ll also need to configure a Stripe webhook. In your Stripe Dashboard → Developers → Webhooks, add an endpoint at https://your-domain.example.com/webhooks/stripe subscribed to the checkout.session.completed event, then copy the signing secret it gives you into STRIPE_WEBHOOK_SECRET . Without this, payments go through on Stripe’s side but the account never gets marked paid — the webhook is what actually activates it, on purpose (see the comment on payment_success() in app.py for why the redirect page alone must never do this).
5. Domain Monitoring — DNS Setup
When a tenant admin adds a domain, they’re shown a TXT record to publish:
Host: _ghostleaks-verify.<their-domain> Type: TXT Value: ghostleaks-verify=<random-token-shown-in-dashboard>

Most DNS providers propagate TXT records within a few minutes, but allow up to 24–48 hours before treating “not verified yet” as a real failure. The verify action re-checks live DNS on demand — there’s no hardcoded waiting period.
Once verified, add the domain’s employee emails before scanning — see README.md for why this matters for scan quality.
6. Scheduled Breach Alerts

GET /send-breach-alerts with header X-Alert-Secret: <ALERT_SECRET> is meant to be called by an external scheduler once a day — a host’s cron/scheduled-job feature, a GitHub Actions scheduled workflow, or an external cron service. The application does not run this on its own; nothing inside the app process triggers it automatically.

It iterates every paid, email-verified user across every tenant, checks their email, and emails them only about new sources found since their last check. The secret is passed as a header rather than a query parameter so it doesn’t end up in server access logs, browser history, or a proxy’s request logs.

Domains can now have employee emails added after verification; each tracked email is checked individually and results are rolled up under the domain. Domains with no employee emails added yet still fall back to the old domain-string search, now clearly labeled as a best-effort fallback rather than the primary mechanism. Security

Fixed: the previous version’s email-check logic returned the actual leaked password for any email address submitted — including other people’s emails, with no ownership verification, up to 100 at a time via bulk CSV upload. Every breach-checking code path now returns only source name, confidence score, and status; no password, hash, or credential value is ever returned. This is enforced at the provider layer, not only in the UI or API response formatting.

Breach Monitoring Web App — Full Source Code Built with Python (Flask), PostgreSQL, and HaveIBeenPwned API

1. Overview GhostLeaks is a cybersecurity SaaS tool that checks whether an email address or password has been exposed in known data breaches. It uses the k-anonymity model (the same approach used by HaveIBeenPwned) so that full passwords or hashes are never transmitted or stored in plaintext.
This package includes the complete, production-ready source code for GhostLeaks, along with setup instructions so you can deploy it on your own server or customize it for your own use case.

Key Features • Email & Password Breach Check — checks credentials against HaveIBeenPwned and BreachDirectory APIs • Bulk CSV Scanning — upload a list of emails and scan them in one go • PDF Report Generation — generates downloadable breach reports (via ReportLab) • User Authentication — secure login/signup system (passwords hashed with bcrypt) • Scan History Dashboard — users can view past scan results • Continuous Monitoring — users can add an API key to enable automatic daily re-checks, with alerts if a new breach is found • Razorpay Payment Integration — ready to enable paid tiers/subscriptions • Modern, Responsive UI — dark navy + terminal-green design system

4. Installation Guide
Step 1 — Extract the Package Unzip the downloaded file into your project folder.
Step 2 — Create a Virtual Environment python3 -m venv venv source venv/bin/activate # On Windows: venv\Scripts\activate
Step 3 — Install Dependencies pip install -r requirements.txt

Step 4 — Configure Environment Variables A file named .env.example is included in the root directory. Copy it and rename it to .env, then fill in your own values: cp .env.example .env # On Windows: copy .env.example .env

Your .env file should contain the following keys: SECRET_KEY=your_secret_key_here DATABASE_URL=postgresql://username:password@host:port/dbname HIBP_API_KEY=your_haveibeenpwned_api_key RAPIDKEY=your_rapidapi_key_for_breachdirectory BREVO_API_KEY=your_brevo_api_key MAIL_USERNAME=your_gmail_address@gmail.com MAIL_PASSWORD=your_gmail_app_password RAZORPAY_KEY_ID=your_razorpay_key_id
RAZORPAY_KEY_SECRET=your_razorpay_key_secret

Note: BREVO_API_KEY is used for transactional emails via Brevo's HTTP API. MAIL_USERNAME and MAIL_PASSWORD are used as a Gmail SMTP fallback if you prefer not to use Brevo — you only need to configure one of the two email methods. For Gmail SMTP, MAIL_PASSWORD must be a Google App Password, not your regular account password.
If you don't plan to enable payments right away, you can leave the Razorpay fields blank — the app will run without them, but the payment feature will not function until they're added.
Step 5 — Set Up the Database This will create all required tables (users, scan_history, etc.) in your PostgreSQL database. flask db upgrade
Step 6 — Run the App Locally flask run
By default, the app will be available at http://127.0.0.1:5000.

5. Deployment (Render Example) 1. Push your code to a GitHub repository. 2. Create a new Web Service on Render. 3. Connect your GitHub repo. 4. Set the build command: pip install -r requirements.txt 5. Set the start command: gunicorn app:app 6. Add all environment variables from Step 4 above in the Render dashboard under Environment. 7. Create a PostgreSQL instance on Render (or use an external provider) and update DATABASE_URL accordingly. 8. Deploy — Render will build and host your app automatically. Note on email delivery: Some free hosting tiers block outbound SMTP traffic on certain ports. This project uses Brevo's HTTP API by default to avoid this issue entirely. The Gmail SMTP option is provided as an alternative and works on most standard hosts, but if you encounter blocked SMTP ports on a free tier, switch to the Brevo API method.

6. Customization Notes Styling: All templates use Jinja2 and are located in the /templates folder. The design system uses CSS variables for colors, defined in /static/css/style.css — update these to re-theme the app.
Breach APIs: The breach-checking logic is in /app/services/breach_check.py. You can swap or add additional breach data sources here.
Payment Tiers: Razorpay integration logic is in /app/routes/payments.py. Update pricing and plan logic here.
Monitoring Frequency: The daily re-check job is handled via a scheduled task — see /app/tasks/monitor.py to adjust frequency or logic.
Email Provider: Email sending logic is in /app/services/email_service.py. It defaults to the Brevo API and falls back to Gmail SMTP if BREVO_API_KEY is not set.
